images.text:
Adam: Mark, can we meet at the coffee shop in front of the job fair in 10 minutes?
Mark: Sure. See you in 10!

Mark: Adam, good to see you.
Adam: Sorry I'm late. I got tied up in another job search workshop.
Mark: What you need to do now is chill. Jobs are being advertised everywhere. People are being recruited. I'm sure you'll land an interview soon.
Adam: Thanks, Mark. The thing I need the most now is to practice some mock interviews.
Mark: I can help with that. The most important thing to remember in an interview is to let them know what you have to offer. A lot of the people I train have been given jobs because they focus on that.

Adam: What I have problems with is some of the questions they ask. This guy once asked me about my nationality.
Mark: I can't believe these questions are still being asked. I know companies who have been penalized because of this discriminatory practice.
Adam: Interviews are stressful enough. One thing I wasn't aware of is that there are illegal interview questions.
Mark: What people need to understand is that they have rights. I'll help you dodge those questions.
Adam: So apart from nationality, what else is illegal to ask?

Mark: Questions about your religion are not permissible.
Adam: It's hard to believe interviewees are being put in a situation where they have to talk about their religious views.
Mark: A lot of these questions are being frowned upon lately. Here's another one: gender. I know people who have been asked if they think a woman can do a particular job effectively.
Adam: Wow. That's inadmissible.
Mark: The list is endless and I could go on for hours.
Adam: Do you think we could focus more on the “do's” and “don't's” in an interview?
Mark: Sure. Let me get some more coffee.

Passive of Present Continuous Tense and Present Perfect Tense
You use the Present Continuous to talk about an action that is happening at the time of speaking. The action or event is in progress.
You use the Present Perfect to talk about a finished action or event with present consequences. There is a connection between what happened in the past and the present.

You often choose the passive form when you want to talk about an action but are not so interested in saying who or what does/did it. Passives without agents (the doers) are common in academic and scientific writing.
Look at the chart below for the structure of the passive voice.

What Clauses and Long Phrases as Subjects
You shift emphasis from the beginning to another part of the sentence by using what, that and who phrases as subjects.

Usually, we focus on the person doing the action in this case.
Example: You really need to relax.

If we wish to place emphasis on another part of the sentence, we isolate that part and package up the rest of the information into a what-phrase (or sometimes a that clause.)
Example: What you really need to do now is relax.

What or Who serves as a placeholder for the content of the noun phrase that has been moved to the end of the sentence. The effect is that more emphasis is placed on the initial content.
Example: What I have problems with is some of the questions they ask.

A “what-phrase” is made up of: what + pronoun + verb phrase
Example:

“What-phrases” are often used to:
  • to introduce a new topic;
  • to give a reason, instruction, or explanation;
  • or to correct something that has been said or done.

Apart from “what-phrases”, we can also use long noun phrases as the subject. A phrase is two or more words and it can include a noun and/or a verb. They are very similar to “what-phrases” but they don't start with “what”.
